title: Interference

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Understand the terms interference and coherence; understand the experiments that demonstrate two-source interference with water waves in a ripple tank, with sound, with light and with microwaves; state the conditions required if two-source interference fringes are to be observed; and recall and use λ = ax / D for double-slit interference using light.

blocks.heading: Interference
blocks.text: Where waves from two sources overlap, the displacements — each point's distance from its rest position — superpose point by point (sub-topic 8.1). Where the two waves arrive in step, with a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, the resultant displacement is large: constructive interference, a maximum. Where they arrive in antiphase, with a path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths, they cancel: destructive interference, a minimum. Interference is this steady pattern of maxima and minima in the overlap region.

blocks.heading: Coherence
blocks.text: Two sources are coherent when they have a constant phase difference, and so the same frequency. With a constant phase difference the maxima and minima stay in fixed places long enough to be seen; sources that drift in and out of step average the pattern away.

blocks.heading: Coherent does not mean in phase
blocks.text: A learner who says coherent sources must be in phase has asked too much. In phase is one special case: phase difference zero, held constant. Two sources holding a steady phase difference of any size — a quarter of a cycle, half a cycle — are coherent and interfere steadily. The test: must the phase difference be zero, or only unchanging? Only unchanging is required.

blocks.heading: Four demonstrations, one pattern
blocks.text: The same pattern is shown by every kind of wave. In a ripple tank, straight wavefronts reach a barrier with two gaps: beyond them the water carries fixed bands of strong and weak oscillation. With sound, two loudspeakers about a metre apart are fed from one signal generator, and a listener walking a line in front of them passes loud and quiet places. With microwaves, a transmitter faces a metal plate bearing two gaps, and a receiver moved along an arc behind them reads alternating strong and weak signals at fixed angles. With light, a double slit is lit by a single lamp and a screen beyond shows bright and dark fringes. In each of these four demonstrations the two sources are coherent, because both are driven by one parent wave.

blocks.heading: Why each pair of sources is coherent
blocks.text: In each demonstration the two sources share one origin. The two gaps in the ripple tank are cut in the path of one set of wavefronts; the two loudspeakers are fed by one signal generator; the two microwave gaps are lit by one transmitter; the two slits of the double slit are lit by one lamp. Each gap or speaker passes on the phase of the single wave that reaches it, so the two sets of waves leave their sources with a phase difference that stays constant. This is the practical reason two-source interference is demonstrated this way: the coherence is arranged at the source, and the pattern in the overlap region then holds steady enough to measure.

blocks.heading: Where the maxima and minima sit
blocks.text: The position of each band follows from the path difference, the difference between the two distances travelled to the point. On the centre line, equidistant from the two sources, the path difference is zero: every wave arrives in step, and the central maximum sits there. One wavelength of path difference to either side gives the next maximum; half a wavelength gives the first minimum. Counting outwards from the centre, the maxima sit at whole numbers of wavelengths and the minima at odd numbers of half wavelengths, which is why the pattern is a set of fixed bands: each band is the set of points that share one path difference.

blocks.heading: The conditions for observable fringes
blocks.text: Two-source fringes are seen when three conditions hold. The sources must be coherent: the same frequency with a constant phase difference. The two waves must arrive with comparable amplitudes — a strong wave and a weak one barely dent each other, so both must come from similar sources and overlap where neither has died away. And the fringe spacing must be wide enough for the eye or detector to resolve, which sets a lower limit on the source spacing for light. Two separate lamps fail the first condition: the phase of the light from each changes abruptly many times each microsecond, so the phase difference between the lamps — and with it every maximum and minimum — changes faster than the eye can register, and the pattern averages away. A double slit lit by a single lamp works because both slits are lit by the same wave train: whatever phase leaves the lamp enters both slits together, so the phase difference at each point, set by the two path lengths, stays constant.

blocks.heading: The double-slit equation
blocks.text: For light, the fringe spacing obeys λ = ax / D, where λ is the wavelength of the light in m, a the separation of the two slits in m, x the distance between the centres of neighbouring bright fringes in m, and D the distance from the slits to the screen in m. Rearranged, x = λD / a: the fringes are wider apart for a longer wavelength, for a screen further away, and for slits closer together. The equation holds for the small angles of a double-slit pattern, where the screen is far from the slits compared with their separation.

blocks.heading: Worked example: red light through a double slit
blocks.text: Red light passes through two slits 0.45 mm apart onto a screen 2.5 m beyond them. Nine gaps between bright fringes span 24.3 mm. Fringe spacing first: x = 24.3 mm ÷ 9 = 2.70 mm. Convert to metres: a = 0.45 mm = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ m and x = 2.70 mm = 2.70 × 10⁻³ m. Equation: λ = ax / D. Substitution: λ = (4.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2.70 × 10⁻³) ÷ 2.5. Now 4.5 × 2.70 = 12.15, so the numerator is 1.215 × 10⁻⁶, and 1.215 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 2.5 = 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ m. So the wavelength is 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ m, given as 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ m to two significant figures — red light, about 490 nm.

blocks.heading: Slit separation, fringe spacing, gaps not fringes
blocks.text: Two lengths in λ = ax / D get confused. The slit separation a is the distance between the two slits — fixed by the slide; the fringe spacing x is the distance between the centres of neighbouring bright fringes on the screen — set by the experiment. And when a span of fringes is measured, the span is divided by the number of gaps between them: twelve bright fringes have eleven gaps between them, so the spacing is the span ÷ 11. The test: count the gaps, not the fringes; and check which length is a and which is x before substituting.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Everything here rests on superposition (8.1) and on the diffraction that lets each slit's wave spread (8.2). The double slit returns as the many-slit grating in 8.4, where a large number of slits sharpens the maxima; the loudspeaker and microwave patterns are the same physics as the light fringes.
